name: Latin
variety: Classical Latin of the late Republic and early Empire in the reconstructed (restored) pronunciation; the ecclesiastical (Italianate) pronunciation is described in the notes. eSpeak NG follows the classical pronunciation.
sources: Allen, W. Sidney (1978). Vox Latina: A Guide to the Pronunciation of Classical Latin. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Allen, W. Sidney (1973). Accent and Rhythm: Prosodic Features of Latin and Greek. Cambridge University Press.
Sturtevant, Edgar H. (1940). The Pronunciation of Greek and Latin. 2nd edition. Philadelphia: Linguistic Society of America.
Weiss, Michael (2009). Outline of the Historical and Comparative Grammar of Latin. Ann Arbor: Beech Stave Press.
McCullagh, Matthew (2011). The sounds of Latin: phonology. In Clackson (ed.), A Companion to the Latin Language. Wiley-Blackwell.
Cser, András (2020). The Phonology of Classical Latin. Transactions of the Philological Society 118, supplement.
contrasts: vowel length for all five vowel qualities (malum 'evil' versus mālum 'apple'; rosa nominative versus rosā ablative; populus 'people' versus pōpulus 'poplar')
single versus geminate consonants (anus 'old woman' versus annus 'year'; ager versus agger)
voiced versus voiceless stops; aspirated stops /pʰ tʰ kʰ/ only in Greek loanwords and a few native words (pulcher)
labialised velars /kʷ ɡʷ/ (written qu, and gu after n) versus velar plus vowel u
syllable weight (light versus heavy) decides the place of the accent and is the basis of verse
/y yː/ and /z/ only in Greek loanwords
allophony: short vowels other than /a/ are more open than the long ones: short i, e, o, u are about [ɪ ɛ ɔ ʊ], long ones [iː eː oː uː] (Allen 1978)
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars, and g before n is [ŋ]: magnus [ˈmaŋnʊs], agnus
word-final m was weak: the preceding vowel was nasalised and lengthened (rosam about [ˈrɔsãː]), and the syllable is elided before a vowel in verse
before ns and nf the vowel is long and nasalised and the n is weak or lost (cōnsul, īnfāns)
/l/ is clear before i and when geminate, dark (velarised) before a consonant, at the end of a word and before back vowels
/r/ is an alveolar trill; /s/ is always voiceless, also between vowels (rosa [ˈrɔsa])
consonantal i between vowels is a geminate glide (maior [ˈmajjɔr], eius [ˈɛjjʊs])
/h/ is weak, does not make position and is dropped between vowels in everyday speech (nihil, mihi)
the diphthong ae moved from [ai̯] to [ae̯] and later to a monophthong [ɛː]; oe is [oe̯]
b before s or t is voiceless (urbs [ʊrps], obtineō [ɔpˈtɪnɛoː])
z in Greek words is [z], double [zz] between vowels
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(ː)(C)(C)(C); a syllable is heavy if it has a long vowel, a diphthong or a coda consonant
phonotactics: a stop plus liquid cluster (muta cum liquida: tr, pr, cr, bl) normally belongs to the following syllable, so a preceding short vowel stays in a light syllable (tenebrae, accent on the first syllable)
x and z count as double consonants and make the preceding syllable heavy
a final vowel, or vowel plus m, is elided before a word that begins with a vowel or h in verse

stress.rule: Words of two syllables are accented on the first; longer words on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy, otherwise on the antepenultimate; an enclitic (-que, -ne, -ve) draws the accent to the syllable before it.
stress.cues: reconstructed as a stress accent for the classical period (Allen 1973, 1978); the older French school took it to be a pitch accent. The acoustic cues cannot be recovered.

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in the classical period as a live process; the weakening of short vowels in medial syllables (facio, conficio) is prehistoric and fixed in the spelling
rhythm.notes: No measurements exist for a language without native speakers. Quantity is contrastive and verse is built on light and heavy syllables (a heavy syllable counts as two light ones), next to a stress accent; final lengthening is an assumption.

length.notes: A long vowel counts as two morae and a short vowel as one; geminate consonants close the preceding syllable. Durations are not recoverable; readers usually make long vowels and geminates about twice as long as short ones.

intonation.declarative: not recoverable; modern readers use a final fall
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particles -ne, num, nonne; the pitch pattern is not recoverable, modern readers use a final rise
intonation.wh_question: question word first; the pitch pattern is not recoverable
intonation.continuation: not recoverable; modern readers use a rise or level pitch at phrase ends
intonation.notes: All entries describe modern reading practice, not evidence about ancient speech.

tone.notes: The Roman grammarians describe the accent in terms taken from Greek pitch accent (acute, circumflex); most modern scholars, following Allen, take the Latin accent to have been one of stress.

problems: vowel length is known only when the text has macrons; plain text, which is the normal case, is read with all vowels short, and the accent rule then moves the stress to the antepenultimate in words with a long penultimate vowel (amicus [ˈamɪkʊs], regina [rˈɛɡɪna], habere [hˈabɛrɛ])
the word list is small (about 300 lines) and gives no vowel lengths for common words
final m is a full [m] (rosam [rˈɔsam]) and n before s, f a full [n] (cōnsul, īnfāns); the nasalised long vowels of the reconstruction are missing
consonantal i is found only at the start of a word and between vowels: coniunx is [kˈɔnɪʊŋks], adiuvō [adˈɪʊwoː], and iam is [ˈɪam]
no devoicing of b before s, t (urbs [ˈʊrbs], obtineō [ɔbtˈɪnɛoː])
aspirated stops are a plain stop followed by a short separate [h] segment, and qu is the sequence [kw]
there is no option for the ecclesiastical pronunciation
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used; elision in verse is not applied
good: the classical values of the letters, after Allen's Vox Latina (cited in the rule file): c and g always velar, v as [w], ae [aɪ], oe [ɔɪ], au, gn as [ŋn], ph th ch aspirated
long and short vowels differ in length (about 150 to 170 against 240 to 270 table units) and in quality (short [ɪ ɛ ɔ ʊ], long [iː eː oː uː])
geminate consonants are lengthened (annus, ille, ecce) and consonantal i between vowels is double (maior [mˈajjɔr])
the accent rule works through the rules for light penultimate syllables (dominus, facilis, agricola on the antepenultimate; monumentum on the penultimate; virumque with the enclitic accent)
l is dark before a consonant and at the end of a word

notes: eSpeak NG follows the classical (restored) pronunciation, not the ecclesiastical one. In the ecclesiastical pronunciation used in church and in much choral music, c and g before e, i, ae, oe are [tʃ] and [dʒ], sc before them is [ʃ], ti before a vowel is [tsi], gn is [ɲɲ], v is [v], ae and oe are [e], h is silent (mihi, nihil with [k]), and vowel length is not distinctive; the place of the accent is the same. The short high vowel of Greek loans is given here as [ʏ] by analogy with the other short vowels.
